text:
Keep the Joined-Up Hand

For a hundred years, children in English-speaking schools learned to write in a flowing, connected script. Today that tradition is under pressure. Keyboards are everywhere, curricula are crowded, and a growing number of teachers and parents ask why seven-year-olds should spend precious hours looping their letters together when a tablet will soon do the job. It is a fair question, and it deserves a fair answer. My answer is that primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting. They should not do it out of nostalgia or a love of neat copperplate. They should do it because the evidence, the practical realities of school life, and the nature of learning itself all point the same way.

Begin with what the opponents of cursive get right. Handwriting is no longer the main way adults produce text. Most of what a child writes after school will be typed. Exams are slowly drifting toward screens. Handwriting instruction can be badly taught, with endless copying of letter shapes and marks given for tidiness rather than thought. And there is a real cost to time. A school day is finite, and every minute spent on letter formation is a minute not spent on reading, number or science. If joined-up writing were merely a decorative skill, I would happily see it go.

But it is not decorative. The strongest argument for it is cognitive. Writing by hand is a different act from typing, and the difference matters most in the years when children are learning to read and spell. When a child forms a letter, the hand must recall the shape, plan the movement, and execute it, all while the mind holds the sound the letter represents. Typing replaces this with a keystroke that looks the same for every letter and requires only recognition, not production. Research using brain imaging has found that handwriting activates networks associated with reading and language in ways that typing does not. Studies of young children who learned letters by writing them, compared with those who typed or traced them, have repeatedly found better letter recognition among the writers. The effect is not enormous, and researchers disagree about how far it generalises, but the direction is consistent and the mechanism is plausible. Making the letter with your own hand helps you know it.

Joined-up writing adds something further. Print, with its separate letters, asks a child to start and stop the pen for every character. Cursive asks the child to think in words. The pen stays on the page, and the movement carries through a whole word as a single gesture. This matters for spelling. A word written in one flow becomes a motor pattern, something the hand learns almost by itself, much as a pianist learns a phrase. Many teachers who favour joined writing report that children who write fluently spell more reliably, because the word is stored as a rhythm as well as a sequence of letters. Again, the research is not conclusive, but the claim fits what we know about how motor memory supports verbal memory.

Then there is speed and fluency, which turn out to be about thinking rather than neatness. A child who must concentrate on forming each letter has less attention left for what they want to say. This is a well-documented problem: slow, effortful handwriting limits the length and quality of children's compositions. Fluent handwriting frees working memory for ideas, grammar and vocabulary. Print can be fluent, but it tends to hit a ceiling because every letter is a separate event. A joined hand, properly taught, is faster for most children, and by the age of eleven or twelve it can keep pace with the speed at which they think. That is the real reason to teach it: not beauty, but bandwidth. Examinations at sixteen are still handwritten for most students, and a pupil who can write legibly at pace for three hours has an advantage that no keyboard skill replaces.

A fourth argument concerns equity. It is tempting to say that technology will fill the gap, and that children can simply be given keyboards. But access to devices, and to the quiet, practised habits that make typing efficient, is unevenly distributed. A pen and paper are cheap and universal. A school that drops handwriting instruction in favour of keyboards risks widening the gap between children whose homes provide a laptop and typing practice and children whose homes do not. Handwriting taught well in school is a skill every child can acquire regardless of what they own. It is also a skill that survives a flat battery, a broken screen, and a classroom with no spare devices.

Opponents will say that print handwriting does everything cursive does, and that joining is an unnecessary extra. The honest answer is that the evidence does not show a dramatic advantage of cursive over well-taught print. Some countries, including Finland, have moved away from compulsory cursive in favour of print and typing, and their literacy results remain strong. I do not want to overstate the case. What I claim is narrower and, I think, more defensible: that a joined, flowing hand is the best-established route to fast, legible, automatic writing, and that its modest cost in teaching time is repaid in fluency. Where schools have a well-designed programme, children typically move from print to joins around the age of seven or eight, and the transition is easy because the foundations are already there. The incremental cost is small. The potential benefit, for children who struggle with spelling or whose writing remains slow, is considerable.

There is also a point about children who find writing hard. For pupils with dyslexia and some other learning differences, a joined script is often recommended precisely because the continuous movement reduces reversals, helps with letter spacing, and makes word boundaries clear. Separate letters invite the b and d confusion that so many children wrestle with, since the two shapes differ only by orientation. In a joined hand, the entry stroke and the flow of the movement help distinguish them. This is not universal, and some children do better with print, but it is a reason not to abandon the joined hand across the board. A school that teaches it can serve those children well, and a school that does not removes a tool that many specialists value.

Finally, consider what we lose if we let it go entirely. Handwriting is a form of personal expression and of cultural continuity. Letters, diaries, signatures, annotations in margins, and the notes passed between friends all carry something of the writer in their shape. A child who never learns a confident, personal hand will still have a voice, but they will have one less way of using it. And they will be unable to read the handwriting of earlier generations, including their own grandparents' letters and the historical documents that remain in archives. Illiteracy in cursive is a quiet loss, but it is a loss.

None of this requires a return to rote drilling or Victorian discipline. The best handwriting teaching is short, frequent and purposeful. Ten minutes a day of well-modelled practice, with attention to posture, pencil grip and movement, is enough for most children. It should be taught alongside, not against, keyboard skills. By the end of primary school, a child should be able to write a page legibly and fluently by hand, and type a page accurately on a keyboard. The two skills are complementary, and a child fluent in both has more options than a child fluent in one.

The case for dropping cursive rests on a picture of the future in which handwriting disappears. That picture is probably wrong. Handwriting is declining as a daily adult habit, but it persists in exams, note-taking, form-filling, and the countless small moments when a pen is simply the quickest tool at hand. Studies of university students suggest that taking notes by hand can improve understanding compared with typing, because the slower pace forces selection and summary. The future is not paperless in the way enthusiasts predicted a generation ago.

So keep the joined-up hand. Teach it briefly, teach it well, and teach it for the right reasons: because it supports reading and spelling, because it frees the mind to compose, because it serves every child whatever their household owns, and because the cost is small. Schools should resist the temptation to treat it as a relic. It is a tool, and for the moment, still one of the most useful that a primary school can put into a child's hand.
